text: The six quality dimensions from Data Quality Management don't get replaced here, training data still has to clear the same bar. What changes is the consequence of failing it, a problem in a report gets read by people who bring judgment, a problem in training data gets learned as a pattern and applied automatically to every future case.

Accuracy, a mislabeled example doesn't just contain one wrong fact, it actively teaches the model the wrong association. Completeness, missing values force assumptions nobody explicitly chose, and missing representation of an entire population segment is its own, more serious failure. Consistency, the same concept recorded two different ways across the set can make the model treat them as genuinely different things.

Validity, an age of two hundred or a negative price doesn't just look wrong, it pulls the model's internal pattern toward nonsense. Uniqueness, duplicate records overweight whatever pattern they represent, and can cause data leakage, where the same record shows up in both training and test data, making results look better than they are. Timeliness, a model trained on stale data learns the world as it was, with no visual cue that its picture of normal is out of date.

A human reading a flawed report can apply skepticism. A model doesn't, it treats the patterns it was trained on as ground truth and extends them confidently to new cases the data never covered. That's garbage in, garbage out, at scale, the output isn't just as bad as the input, it's the input's flaw generalized and repeated indefinitely.

Good enough for a report and good enough to train on are different bars, even using the same six dimensions. Next up: bias in data, where dimension failures and population mismatches actually produce unfair outcomes.
